newsitem.title: USA: GFOA "deeply troubled" about flow control session.
newsitem.headline: GFOA "deeply troubled" about flow control session.

text.p: Thirty-two finance officers from 23 states told the U.S. Congress they are "deeply troubled" that some key panel chairmen are questioning the need for a law to protect existing flow control sites.

The finance officers, in written testimony coordinated by the Government Finance Officers Association, referred to March 18 statements by Sen. John Chafee, R-R.I., chairman of the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, and Sen. Bob Smith, R-N.H., chairman of the Environment Committee's subpanel on waste control, at a hearing on the issue.

Smith had said that backers of federal flow-control legislation "have a much tougher case to prove this year" because earlier dire warnings of widespread defaults of waste facility bonds never materialized.

Chafee had said that most of the 18 credit rating downgrades since the U.S. Supreme Court's 1994 finding that flow control is unconstitutional occurred in the first year after the decision. "Relatively few have occurred in the two years since," he said.
But finance officers said on Wednesday that Congress is wrong to think that legislation is not needed because there have been no defaults or cutoffs of debt service payments.
"Default and bankruptcy are options of last resort and are not entered into unless all other financial alternatives have been exhausted," finance officers said.
The fact that there have been no defaults does not mean "that jurisdictions are not experiencing severe financial hardships," they said.
The finance officers reacted to a statement by U.S. Rep. Bill Pascrell, D-N.J., at the March 18 hearing that Congress should "bury flow control legislation in the trash heap of discarded ideas."
Pascrell also charged that some New Jersey counties have bonded for facilities that were never built.
The finance officers said issuing bonds without constructing a project is a "rather unusual occurrence in the municipal market, which could have serious financial repurcussions for an issuer."
They also said that people who suggested at the hearing that solid waste issuers are "awash with cash" are misinformed.
"The economics of the industry at the time many of these facilities were financed justified the rate levels that were established," the group said.
Finance officers also challenges suggestions that flow control is not necessary because it permits underwriters to support facilities that are poor investments.
"To suggest that underwriters ramrod inappropriate projects through this process oversimplifies the complexity and expense involved in bringing a bond issuer to market," they said.
